title: RepairLab Appointment Clarification and Recovery
abstract: RepairLab is a local browser prototype for people who need to cancel one of several appointments through a conversational assistant. Its interaction problem is referential ambiguity: a request such as 'cancel my appointment' does not identify a unique record. The project develops the earlier literature-review question into inspectable behaviour rather than claiming that one clarification strategy is already superior. It provides general repetition, a targeted question and selectable candidate appointments, while retaining the same fictional schedule and action controller. A deliberate omission condition removes Friday physiotherapy from the first candidate list, allowing the user to reject the suggestions and identify it through free text. Every proposed cancellation is displayed before confirmation; correction, stopping and undo remain available. HTML, CSS and JavaScript implement the interface and state transitions. Interpretation uses transparent lexical rules, while provider integration and uncertain language understanding are simulated or absent. Twenty-five automated checks and browser walkthroughs examine cancellation boundaries and recovery paths. These establish functional behaviour, not usability, cognitive-load reduction or comparative effectiveness. The contribution is a reproducible demonstration of clarification with an escape from incorrect candidates, suitable for subsequent controlled evaluation.

sections.heading: Problem and scope
paragraphs: The target user is an adult managing several appointments in a text interface. At the cancellation step, an underspecified reference can lead to repeated requests or selection of the wrong record. Stoyanchev, Liu and Hirschberg (2014, introduction) distinguish generic requests to repeat from targeted questions that identify the missing information. Their work supports treating repair as an interaction problem, although its speech-recognition setting does not establish the frequency of appointment ambiguity. RepairLab uses a fictional scenario to investigate the design opportunity, not to claim evidence from real patients.

The scope is cancellation of three fictional December 2026 appointments. Booking, medical advice, authentication, live providers and persistent personal profiles are excluded. The previous review asked whether options outperform repetition. This implementation separates a more modest question: can users inspect an interpretation and recover when its candidates exclude their intention? The supplied A1 rubric foregrounds context, checked citations and a traceable contribution. Accordingly, each design decision below connects a specific difficulty to a source and observable behaviour. No unpublished marker explanation is assumed.

sections.heading: Design rationale
paragraphs: Three strategy settings share the same records and execution controller. General repetition asks the user to restate the request; the targeted condition asks which service, date or ID is intended; candidate mode displays appointment buttons. Bohus and Rudnicky (2005, Table 1) distinguish repetition, reprompting and example-based help, so these are not treated as interchangeable. Separating the conditions makes their wording inspectable, but no participant comparison was conducted. The schedule remains visible in every condition, meaning this is a hybrid interface rather than a pure speech comparison.

Candidates show service, day and time, while the schedule retains dates and IDs. This applies recognition over recall from Lecture 05: users can compare visible records rather than remember a spoken list. Hu et al. (2020, Figure 1) demonstrate clarification using selectable intent labels, motivating the interaction pattern. RepairLab does not reproduce their reinforcement-learning method or its reported gains. Candidate order is fixed, and the two-record omission condition is deliberately configured; it is not evidence that a model naturally made this error.

The candidate list includes 'None of these' and accepts an identifier outside the displayed set. Rejection clears the candidates without deleting the conversation or changing appointments. This operationalises efficient correction, G9, and disambiguation under uncertainty, G10 (Amershi et al., 2019, Table 1). Grounding becomes checkable because the assistant displays the interpreted record. For example, rejecting Tuesday and Thursday, then entering 'Friday', produces a physiotherapy preview. This is a recoverable interaction, not proof that an escape option reduces cognitive load.

A cancellation requires a separate confirmation button after the preview states the service, date, time and ID. 'Go back and correct' discards the pending interpretation; 'Stop request' ends the request. Lecture 06's evaluation gulf motivates showing what will happen, and Lecture 07's confirm and correct turns motivate the recovery controls. The controller checks that the record is still active before changing it. A completion message names the changed record and offers undo. These mechanisms support visibility and reversibility without claiming that confirmation alone prevents misunderstanding. Lecture 12 (slides 8 and 12) supports checking preconditions and exposing arguments before execution. Consuming the pending confirmation once makes repeated confirmation harmless within this session; it is not durable, cross-session idempotency.

Capability disclosure appears before interaction and in unsupported-action replies, applying G1 (Amershi et al., 2019). Users are told that records are fictional and interpretation is rule-based. Clear phase labels distinguish clarification, pending confirmation and completion. The event view exposes processing order for inspection; it does not present step numbers as latency measurements. This follows Lecture 04's emphasis on feedback and Lecture 08's distinction between generating a statement and successfully executing an action. The prototype never contacts a provider. Following Lecture 12 (slides 13-14), completion text is constructed after the local state change, rather than trusting a generated success claim.

sections.heading: Architecture and developed interaction
paragraphs: The system diagram separates the browser interface, lexical interpreter, in-memory appointment collection, repair policy and action controller. The interpreter matches known service aliases, dates and IDs; zero or multiple matches do not authorise cancellation. The session state contains the strategy, candidates, pending identifier and recent undoable action. No hidden long-term memory or retrieved web content is used. Text enters the page as text nodes, and the controller accepts only known record IDs. This bounded architecture makes the simulated intelligent behaviour reproducible while leaving realistic language understanding unimplemented. Lecture 10 distinguishes information supplied for the current task from persistent personal memory: resetting this session removes its state, rather than simulating human forgetting. Lecture 11 asks whether retrieval is needed. Exact lookup over three supplied records is sufficient here; visible IDs connect the interpretation to its source record, but this is neither vector retrieval nor evidence that every possible appointment is covered.

The three storyboards are generated from functional replays of the same core used by the interface. The first follows candidate selection through confirmation and undo. The second rejects an incomplete list and identifies the omitted appointment. The third replaces a dental preview with an eye appointment before committing. The frames distinguish user actions, system replies and record status. A browser screenshot separately documents the developed interface rather than presenting a conceptual sketch as a working screen.

sections.heading: Development evidence and limitations
paragraphs: Development was recorded in actual local commits: the core and behavioural checks were created first, followed by the interface, then replay evidence and source boundaries. Twenty-five automated checks cover ambiguity, omitted candidates, invalid IDs, unsupported actions, correction, stop, duplicate confirmation, stale previews, isolated sessions and undo. Browser walkthroughs also verified the three strategy prompts, confirmation, undo and omission recovery. Five replay traces and the test output are supplied in the repository. These checks establish specified transitions; they do not measure human preference, task success or effort.

The current limitations are substantial. Lexical matching lacks robust negation, paraphrase and multilingual understanding. The visible schedule may make repair easier than in a standalone assistant, and deliberate omission differs from natural ranking errors. Only one recent cancellation is undoable, and refresh loses session state. Future work would compare the three strategies on matched tasks, including incorrect candidates, while measuring correct interpretation and perceived effort separately. AI assistance and the inspection steps are disclosed in the README.
